title: Kanban vs Scrum: Differences and How to Choose

titles: Kanban vs Scrum: Differences and How to Choose
Kanban vs Scrum: How to Pick for Your Team
Kanban vs Scrum for Team Leads Running Many Projects
brief.h1: Kanban vs Scrum: Differences and How to Choose
brief.metaDescription: Kanban vs scrum explained for team leads: how each works, how they differ, and how to pick one, or both, for the projects you run.
brief.searchIntent: The searcher wants to know how Kanban and Scrum differ and which one fits their team. A clear explainer with a side by side table, when-to-use guidance and a way to decide serves them best.
brief.reader: Team leads at companies with 10 to 200 people who run several projects at once. They have heard both terms and may already use a board or hold sprints. They want to decide which method, or mix, to try on their next project and how to start.
brief.angle: Most top pages ask you to pick one method for the whole team. We help a team lead decide per project, using how predictable the work is and how often priorities change, and we show when a mix such as Scrumban makes sense.

outline.h2: Kanban vs Scrum in one minute
points: Kanban is a visual method that helps you see tasks and cut inefficiencies, while Scrum gives structure to the team and the schedule.
Coursera puts it this way: one optimizes flow and the other optimizes iteration.
Both are Agile frameworks that aim to improve team efficiency and adapt to change.
Atlassian says neither wins by default and the right choice depends on how predictable your workflow is, how often priorities shift and how your team likes to work.
Tell the reader we will cover definitions, a side by side table, when to use each, how to combine them and a short quiz.
Open with a plain definition: Kanban is a visual project management method where work moves across a board with columns for each stage, and tasks sit on cards.
Explain what the board shows: where tasks are piling up, which helps you decide where to put people.
Kanban means signboard in Japanese and started with cards that tracked production at a Toyota factory. Asana credits Taiichi Ohno in the 1940s.
Work is pulled: a person takes a new task only when the previous one is done, and there are no required roles.

h3.title: How a Kanban board works
points: Typical columns are to do, in progress and done, and cards can show assignee, due date and tags.
Teams can use a cumulative flow diagram to find where work piles up.

h3.title: What WIP limits do
points: Work in progress limits cap the number of items in each stage, which prevents overload and improves throughput.
Kanban teams track cycle time and lead time.
Open with a plain definition: Scrum is an Agile framework where a team works in fixed-length sprints toward a shared goal.
Scrum was first described in the 1986 paper "New New Product Development Game" by Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka, according to Planview.
Explain the cycle: the team picks work from its backlog for a time-boxed sprint, works toward a sprint goal, then reviews the result and improves its process before the next sprint.
Sprints commonly run one to four weeks.
Name the roles Atlassian lists (Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers) and the regular events: sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review and retrospective.
Measure progress with velocity, sprint goal progress and burndown charts.

outline.h2: Kanban vs Scrum: the main differences
points: Present a side by side table with rows for workflow style, roles, planning cadence, handling change, capacity control, metrics and release style.
Workflow: Kanban moves in continuous flow and Scrum in fixed sprints.
Roles: Kanban has no required roles, while Scrum has defined accountabilities.
Change: Kanban lets priorities change as work moves, while Scrum considers changes against the sprint goal and discourages them mid sprint.
Capacity: Kanban uses WIP limits, while Scrum uses sprint commitment and team capacity.
Metrics: cycle time, lead time and throughput for Kanban, versus velocity and burndown for Scrum.
Add Planview's note that in Scrum a delay can halt the whole plan because activities share one cadence.

outline.h2: When to use Kanban and when to use Scrum
points: Give the reader a short rule: match the method to how predictable the work is.
Planview says Kanban suits projects with widely varying priorities, and Scrum suits teams with stable priorities.

h3.title: Kanban fits when
points: Work arrives as ongoing requests or priorities shift often.
You want to see bottlenecks without changing your whole process, as Coursera notes.
Work can ship when it is ready.

h3.title: Scrum fits when
points: You can break an outcome into small usable increments and review each one at the end of a sprint.
The team benefits from a steady rhythm, explicit sprint goals and a regular chance to inspect its work.
Priorities stay fairly stable and you want clear roles.

outline.h2: Can you use Kanban and Scrum together?
points: Yes: the hybrid is called Scrumban.
Coursera cites the 2022 State of Agile report: 27 percent of respondents used Scrumban and 56 percent used Kanban.
Planview says many Scrum teams add a Kanban board for extra visibility, and Kanban can show the flow of work whatever method the team follows.
Coursera's takeaway: you can get both continuous visibility and structured iteration without choosing only one.
Say what a mix looks like in practice: keep sprints, and use a board with WIP limits to spot where work piles up.

outline.h2: How to choose when you run several projects
points: Decide per project, not per company: one team lead can run a request-driven project on Kanban and a roadmap project on Scrum.
Use the three questions from Atlassian: how predictable is the workflow, how often do priorities shift, and how does your team like to work and learn.
Ask whether you want required roles and fixed meetings or a lighter setup.
Point to Scrumban when answers split across both methods.
Introduce the quiz that follows.

outline.h2: Try one method on one project this week
points: Pick one project and run the chosen method for a single cycle before changing anything else.
Kanban start: draw columns for to do, in progress and done, then find where work piles up and set a WIP limit there.
Scrum start: pick a sprint length between one and four weeks, choose work from the backlog, set a sprint goal and hold a review at the end.
Look back after one cycle and adjust, and add a board to a Scrum project if you want more visibility.

gaps: Top pages ask the reader to pick one method for the whole team, and none speak to a lead who runs several projects at once. We show how to choose per project.
No top page gives the reader a quick decision tool. We add a short quiz built on Atlassian's three decision factors.
The pages explain Scrum's structure but rarely say plainly what happens when something slips. Planview notes a delay can halt the whole plan, and we say so.
Pages describe Scrumban in a line. We explain what a mix looks like and give the 2022 State of Agile numbers that Coursera cites.
Few pages give a first step. We end with a one cycle trial for Kanban and for Scrum.
Sources differ on small points, such as how much Scrum rules out changes mid sprint. We use the careful wording and flag the rest for an editor.

faqs.question: Is Kanban or Scrum better?
faqs.answer: Neither is better by default. The answer must say the choice depends on how predictable the work is, how often priorities change and how the team likes to work, with Kanban for flow and Scrum for fixed sprints.

faqs.question: Why use Kanban instead of Scrum?
faqs.answer: Kanban fits ongoing requests and changing priorities because work flows continuously and there are no required roles. Say it also shows where work piles up without changing your whole process.

faqs.question: What is Scrumban?
faqs.answer: Scrumban is a hybrid that combines Scrum and Kanban. Mention the 2022 State of Agile numbers: 27 percent of respondents used Scrumban and 56 percent used Kanban, as cited by Coursera.

faqs.question: Can a team use Kanban and Scrum at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Say Scrum teams often add a Kanban board for visibility, and Kanban can be used with any method to visualize the flow of work.

faqs.question: Is Jira a Kanban tool?
faqs.answer: Kanban is a method, and Jira is software that can be used for it. Say Atlassian offers a free Jira Kanban template, and keep the answer short and neutral.

blocks.text: If you lead a team that runs several projects at once, you've probably heard both terms and wondered which one fits your next project. Kanban vs scrum is a common debate, and it can feel like you have to choose one side for the whole team.
Thankfully, you don't have to, because the right choice depends on your work and your team, as [Atlassian explains](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum).
In this guide, we'll walk you through the following so you can decide per project and start with a small trial this week:

items: What each method is, with a plain definition of Kanban and of Scrum.
How the two differ, shown side by side in a table.
When to use each one, and when a mix makes sense.
A short quiz that helps you choose for your next project.

sections.h2: Kanban vs Scrum in one minute

blocks.text: Kanban is a visual method that helps you [see your tasks and cut inefficiencies](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum), while Scrum gives structure to the team and the schedule. If you want a quick refresher on the wider field first, our [project management basics](https://planwise.example/blog/project-management-basics) page covers it.

Coursera puts it this way: [one method optimizes flow and the other optimizes iteration](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum). Both are Agile frameworks, and both aim to [improve team efficiency and help you adapt to change](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum).
Atlassian says neither method wins by default, and the right choice depends on a few things about your work and your team.

items: How predictable your workflow is.
How often your priorities shift.
How your team likes to work and learn.

blocks.text: As you can see, the right choice depends on your projects, so we suggest looking at each one on its own rather than picking a method for the whole team. [Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum) makes the same point, and it's why we suggest looking at each project on its own.
Here's what we'll cover so you can find your answer quickly:

items: What Kanban and Scrum each are, in plain words.
A side by side table of the main differences.
When to use Kanban and when to use Scrum.
How to combine the two.
A short quiz to help you decide for your own project.

blocks.text: Work moves across a board with a column for each stage, and the tasks are written on cards.
The board shows you where tasks are piling up, which helps you decide where to put your people. For a deeper walk-through, see [our Kanban guide](https://planwise.example/blog/kanban-guide).

The word Kanban means "signboard" in Japanese, and the method started with [cards that tracked production progress in a Toyota factory](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum). [Asana credits Taiichi Ohno](https://asana.com/resources/waterfall-agile-kanban-scrum) with developing the framework at Toyota in the 1940s, though we suggest confirming that before you repeat it.

Kanban uses a [pull system](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/), so a person takes on a new task only after the previous one is complete. Planview adds that Kanban has no pre-defined roles, although a Project Manager may still be involved, and the team is encouraged to pitch in when any one person is overwhelmed.
How a Kanban board works

On a Kanban board, columns stand for the stages of work, and [cards show which stage each task is in](https://asana.com/resources/waterfall-agile-kanban-scrum). Here is what a card can tell you at a glance:

items: The card shows the task or deliverable itself.
The card names the person the task is assigned to.
The card lists due dates and time frames.
The card carries tags, such as priority or task type.

blocks.text: Typical columns are to do, in progress and done. Teams can also use a [cumulative flow diagram](https://asana.com/resources/waterfall-agile-kanban-scrum) to find where work is piling up.
What WIP limits do

Work in progress limits, often called [WIP limits](https://asana.com/resources/waterfall-agile-kanban-scrum), cap the number of work items allowed in each stage. This prevents overload and improves throughput, which means your team finishes work before it starts more.
Watching these two numbers over time gives you a simple way to check how your process is doing.

Scrum is an Agile framework where a team works in fixed-length sprints toward a shared goal. [Planview](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) traces Scrum to the 1986 paper "New New Product Development Game" by Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka.

According to [Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum), a Scrum cycle runs like this: The team selects work from its backlog for a time-boxed sprint, works toward a sprint goal, then reviews the result and improves its process before the next sprint.
Sprints commonly run [one to four weeks](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum), so you can pick a length that fits how often you want to check the work.
Scrum roles and events

items: The Product Owner is one of the three Scrum accountabilities.
The Scrum Master is the second accountability.
The Developers hold the third accountability.

blocks.text: How Scrum measures progress

[Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum) says Scrum teams track sprint goal progress, velocity and burndown charts. As you can see, these measures all focus on what the team finishes within a sprint, which matches the fixed rhythm Scrum is built around.

sections.h2: Kanban vs Scrum: the main differences

blocks.text: You can scan the table below before you read the details. We built it from [Atlassian's comparison](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum), so each row shows how the two methods line up on one part of the work.

rows: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers
Priorities can change as work moves through the system
Changes are considered against the sprint goal
WIP limits for active workflow stages
Lead time, cycle time, throughput and cumulative flow
Sprint goal progress, velocity and burndown charts
Work can release when it is ready
Often planned around sprint or release goals

blocks.text: As you can see, the biggest gap is rhythm: Kanban lets you [change priorities as work moves](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum), while Scrum weighs each change against the sprint goal. Planview adds that Scrum [discourages changes during the sprint](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/), though the sources word this a little differently, so check how your own team handles it.

If you run several projects at once, Planview makes a useful point about delays. In Scrum, [all activities happen on the same cadence according to the project plan](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/), so if there is a delay, the entire project may come to a halt.
Honestly, that difference alone can settle the choice for a project where delays are common, such as a request queue that never stops.

sections.h2: When to use Kanban and when to use Scrum

blocks.text: The simplest way to choose is to match the method to how predictable the work is. If you run several projects at once, you can make this call for each project instead of picking one method for the whole team.

Planview says [Kanban is best for projects with widely varying priorities](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/), while Scrum is best for teams with stable priorities that may not change much over time. Atlassian adds that [the right choice depends on how predictable your workflow is and how often priorities shift](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum).
Kanban fits when

items: Work arrives as ongoing requests, or priorities shift often.
You want to see bottlenecks without changing your whole process, as [Coursera notes](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum).
Work can ship as soon as it is ready.

blocks.text: Atlassian describes Kanban as a fit for [teams with ongoing requests or frequently shifting priorities](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum). For example, a support queue or a stream of small design requests rarely waits neatly for the next sprint.
Scrum fits when

items: You can break an outcome into small usable increments and review each one at the end of a sprint.
The team benefits from a steady rhythm, explicit sprint goals and a regular chance to inspect its work.
Priorities stay fairly stable, and you want clear roles.

blocks.text: Atlassian says Scrum suits teams that [benefit from a steady delivery rhythm and explicit sprint goals](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum). To test this, ask whether a two-week plan is likely to still hold in two weeks, and if it is, Scrum has room to work. If it is, Scrum has room to work.

sections.h2: Can you use Kanban and Scrum together?

blocks.text: Yes, you can, and many teams do, using a hybrid called **Scrumban** that borrows ideas from both methods so you don't have to choose only one. The hybrid is called **Scrumban**, and it lets you use ideas from both methods so you don't have to choose only one.

Coursera cites the 2022 State of Agile report, which found that [27 percent of respondents used Scrumban and 56 percent used Kanban](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum). Mixing the two is a common choice among teams that want both structure and flexibility, which fits many leads who run several projects at once.

Planview says [many Scrum teams add a Kanban board](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) to get an extra layer of visibility on their projects. It also notes that Kanban can show the flow of work whatever method the team uses to do it.
Coursera's takeaway is that you can get [both continuous visibility and structured iteration](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum) without having to pick only one method.
In practice, a mix looks like this:

items: Keep your sprints, your sprint goal and the regular reviews that give your team a steady rhythm.
Put the sprint work on a board with columns for each stage, such as to do, in progress and done.
Set WIP limits on the stages where work tends to pile up, so the team finishes items before it starts new ones.

blocks.text: If you want to try the board side of this mix, [Kanban boards in Planwise](https://planwise.example/features/kanban) are an easy place to start.

sections.h2: How to choose when you run several projects

blocks.text: The best way to pick between these two methods is to ask which one each project needs, because the choice doesn't have to cover your whole company. If you run several projects at once, you can match the method to the work in front of you.

For example, one project might be a stream of ongoing requests where priorities shift often. [Planview](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) says Kanban suits projects with widely varying priorities, while Scrum suits teams with stable priorities, so you could run the first on Kanban and a roadmap project on Scrum.

[Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum) says the right choice depends on how predictable your workflow is, how often priorities shift and your preferred way of working and learning. You can turn those factors into questions for each project:

items: How predictable is the workflow, and can you break it into small pieces that you plan ahead?
How often do priorities change once work has started?
How does your team like to work and learn, with a steady rhythm of planning and review or with a looser flow?
Do you want required roles and fixed meetings, or a lighter setup?

blocks.text: On that last question, [Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum) notes that Kanban has no required roles, while Scrum has defined accountabilities.

If your answers split across both methods, Scrumban is worth a look, and we covered it above. You can also read our guide to [Agile for small teams](https://planwise.example/blog/agile-for-small-teams), and the short quiz below turns your answers into a suggestion for each project.

sections.h2: Try one method on one project this week

blocks.text: You don't need to change how your whole team works to find out which method fits. Pick one project and run the chosen method for a single cycle before you change anything else.
A small test teaches you more than a long debate, and you can compare how the project feels against your others.
If you chose Kanban, you can start with these steps:

items: Draw three columns for to do, in progress and done, as [Asana describes](https://asana.com/resources/waterfall-agile-kanban-scrum) the typical stages of a board.
Put each task on a card and place it in the column that matches where it stands today.
Look at where cards are piling up, since [Asana notes](https://asana.com/resources/waterfall-agile-kanban-scrum) that teams find bottlenecks this way and then set work in progress limits.
Set a WIP limit on the stage where work piles up, which caps the number of items there and helps prevent overload.

blocks.text: If you chose Scrum, you can start with these steps:

items: Pick a sprint length between one and four weeks, which is the range [Atlassian says](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum) sprints commonly run.
Choose the work for the sprint from your backlog.
Write a sprint goal so the whole team knows what it is working toward.
Hold a review at the end of the sprint to look at the result and improve your process before the next one.

blocks.text: After one cycle, look back at what worked and adjust before you change anything else on the project. If you ran Scrum and want more visibility, you can add a board, because [Planview says](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) many Scrum teams use Kanban to add an extra layer of visibility to their projects.
Set up a Kanban board for your busiest project in Planwise and see where work piles up this week.
Is Kanban or Scrum better?

Neither is better by default, and [Atlassian says](https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/kanban-vs-scrum) the right choice depends on how predictable your workflow is, how often priorities shift and how your team likes to work and learn.
Kanban fits continuous flow, while Scrum fits fixed-length sprints, so you can match each method to the project in front of you.
Why use Kanban instead of Scrum?
Planview also says Kanban is [best for projects with widely varying priorities](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).
Coursera adds that Kanban makes work visible, so you can [spot bottlenecks early and improve flow without changing your entire process](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum).
What is Scrumban?
Scrumban is a hybrid that combines Scrum and Kanban, and Coursera notes that Kanban is [often used in tandem with Scrum](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum) this way.
Coursera also cites the 2022 State of Agile report, in which [27 percent of respondents were using Scrumban and 56 percent were using Kanban](https://www.coursera.org/articles/kanban-vs-scrum).
Can a team use Kanban and Scrum at the same time?

Yes, you can, because Planview says [many Scrum teams use Kanban as a visual tool](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/) to add an extra layer of visibility to their projects.

Kanban can also be applied to visualize and improve the flow of work, [regardless of the methodology being used to do the work](https://www.planview.com/resources/guide/introduction-to-kanban/kanban-vs-scrum/).
